pr_body:
This PR adds a C99 stdio value formatter capability named `cbprintf()` (plus related variants) where generated text is emitted through a callback.  This allows generation of arbitrarily long output without a buffer, functionality that is core to printk, logging, and other system and application needs.

The formatter supports most C99 specifications, excluding:
* %L[aefg] long double conversion
* wide character output

The new solution is derived from `z_prf()`, which had the most complete functionality available.  Format parsing has been reimplemented, while floating point conversion has been retained and enhanced.

Kconfig options allow disabling features like floating-point conversion if they are not necessary.

Benefits include:
* No more inconsistencies between printk, logging, and shell formatting capabilities.
* Reduced inconsistencies due to toolchain libc capabilities.
* Simplified (toolchain-independent) formatting feature selection via Kconfig.
* Core infrastructure can avoid duplication with libc printf by using cbprintf variants.
* Potentially a path to resolving #18351 and related issues, as the infrastructure can tell a caller the total size of arguments to the conversion string.
* Fixed bugs with several specifications.

Costs include:
* Applications that used only printk with no extra features consume more code space than the previous implementation.

Fixes #29202

```
+/* We can't determine at build-time whether int is 64-bit, so assume
+ * it is.  If not the values are truncated at build time, and the str
+ * pointers will be updated during test initialization.
+ */
+static const unsigned int pfx_val = (unsigned int)0x7b6b5b4b3b2b1b0b;
```

In the Zephyr environment, an int is always 32 bits. Only a long will 
vary in width, and sizeof(long) is always equal to sizeof(void*). So the 
constant above will always be truncated.

> it increases the ROM footprint of `samples/hello_world` from 15760 to 16992 ... Is there something we can do about this?

Yeah, that's the fly in the ointment.  I've done a bunch of measurements, and tried different things, but have found nothing more that can be made optional without causing breakage (e.g. failing to correctly deduce the size of an argument that can't be converted, causing subsequent conversions to be corrupted).  Disabling 64-bit integer handling has no significant effect: the cost is all in handling C99 format specifications correctly.

Once you start adding logging and shell and other things that used to use two implementations the impact goes down.  At least one sensor sample I tried shrunk with this.  There's also some opportunity to eliminate existing dependencies on libc in Zephyr code, since this provides a replacement for `snprintf`.

The only candidate solution remaining is to have a Kconfig option that uses the old `z_vprintk()` implementation.  That's small, and would satisfy the needs of `hello_world` and anything that only uses `printk`, doesn't care about floating point, precision options, or decimal 64-bit values.

I'll take a look at what happens with that.

This adds `cb[v]snprintf()` as a substitute for `[v]snprintf()` to avoid pulling in libc formatting code when Zephyr modules need format-to-buffer capability.  With that name policy `cb[v]printf` should be substitutes for `[v]printf`, but those names are already used for the new API that takes the callback function and context.

I'm not a fan of trying to override standard library functions, so some options are:
* do not provide something that can replace `[v](sn)?printf()` using the internal cbprintf infrastructure;
* move the `cb` part of the substitute API to the end of the identifier, e.g. `printfcb("fmt", ...)` and `snprintfcb(buf,sz,fmt,...)`

I'm inclined to try the latter.

> This is opt-in, but if selected the size of `hello_world` is unchanged.

While this was true when I wrote it, it's not exactly true now.  To use the former `v_printk()` to implement `cbsnprintf` it is necessary to adapt it to count the number of characters that would be emitted.  This increases the image size from 15738 (pre-PR) to 15866 (with `CONFIG_CBPRINTF_NANO`).  The size with `CONFIG_CBPRINTF_COMPLETE` is 16958.

If we make the `[v](sn)?printf` replacement functions optional most of that 128 bytes could probably be reclaimed.  I'll tackle that later.

I've:
* removed the FULL_WIDTH option;
* combined the former pad0_prefix (integer-only) , pad0_pre_dp, and
  pad0_post_dep values into one field pad0_value with a bit field to
  distinguish which of the floating point positions would use it;
* used unions because width and pad0_prefix have disjoint lifespans,
  as do prec and pad0_pre_exp.

I also moved the conversion specifier out of the bitfield to a char,
because it turns out the compiler's wise enough to use the leftover
bitfield space to store it anyway.  So the conversion specification
structure is three words (12 bytes on a I32 host).

Both these changes reduced code size.

cbprintf now consistently formats non-null `%p` as `0x1234`, no leading zeros.

Format of null pointers diverges: `COMPLETE` uses `(nil)` following Linux libc, while `NANO` uses `0x0` because detecting null and emitting `(nil)` increases memory significantly from the previous footprint.

`CBPRINTF_NULL_AS_NIL` has been removed.

When `MINIMAL_LIBC` is selected `CBPRINTF_NANO` selects `LIBC_SUBSTS` which causes a size increase, but this is required to correctly implement `s[n]printf()` (otherwise the number of characters that would have been written is not counted.)

 A warning call-out has been added to the documentation to note the limitations of C library functions when `MINIMAL_LIBC` is combined width `CBPRINTF_NANO`.  `tests/libc/sprintf` should now pass with that combination but this is a non-default configuration that requires manual checking with an overlay, and when used some tests are skipped because they verify unsupported functionality. 

Floating point formatting support is default-enabled with `FPU` is selected, as this seems to be the clue that floating point is desired by the application.

This looks fine to me.

> Format of null pointers diverges: `COMPLETE` uses `(nil)` following Linux libc, while `NANO` uses `0x0` because detecting null and emitting `(nil)` increases memory significantly from the previous footprint.

That much? I would have expected 10-15 bytes of text.

I'll try to come up with a good comment to replace the `/* Magically convert the base-2 exponent to a base-10exponent. */` eventually.

I can see potential for smallish code size reduction here and there but that'll be easier to test once this is merged.

@nashif you may turn that -1 on my behalf to +1.

> > Format of null pointers diverges: `COMPLETE` uses `(nil)` following Linux libc, while `NANO` uses `0x0` because detecting null and emitting `(nil)` increases memory significantly from the previous footprint.
> That much? I would have expected 10-15 bytes of text.

That motivated me to try harder, and by refactoring a little it's only 12 bytes more.  So that difference has been removed: both `COMPLETE` and `NANO` format null pointers as `(nil)`.

> If you prefer we can eliminate these complaints by (a) not being prepared to support ILP64, and/or (b) not testing handling of undefined format combinations.  But I'd rather just ignore checkpatch's whingeing.

ILP64 should probably be considered only the day they're needed.

There are many more code instances where such considerations would be 
required. Better do that all at once in a unified way.

IMHO of course.

issue_context.title: core kernel depends on minimal libc `z_prf()`
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
Some dependencies have accumulated on the internal minimal libc function `z_prf()`, to the point where the function was moved out of minimal libc and into lib/os.

This is not good, lib/os now has two completely orthogonal printf()-like implementations that we will have to maintain in perpetuity, even if minimal libc is not used, and especially if we ever settle on a different third-party small-footprint C library and remove minimal libc entirely.

Any kernel subsystem dependency on `z_prf()` needs to use the `printk()` family of functions instead. If `printk()` needs to support some functionality that is only offered by `z_prf()` (like printing floating point values) add non-default Kconfigs against printk() code which adds this and has negligible footprint or stack space impact on users who don't enable it.

`z_prf()` itself needs to be moved back to minimal libc where it belongs.

review_comments: Think this needs some adjustment, based on CI results.
Yes, I'd missed the change to the pointer format in that test.

> We can't determine at build-time whether int is 64-bit, so assume

how about `BUILD_ASSERT(sizeof(int) < 8)`?

The below casting where you do stuff like
```
	static const unsigned int pfx_val = (unsigned int)0x7b6b5b4b3b2b1b0b;
```

Are you sure that this is defined behavior?
This is generating a CI lintian warning BTW

I'm not trying to test whether sizeof(int) < 8, I'm trying to support sizeof(int) == 8, in the belief that someday somebody might want Zephyr to run on some DSP-like ILP64 system.

The diagnostic is

    WARNING:TYPECAST_INT_CONSTANT: Unnecessary typecast of c90 int constant

but in fact it is necessary to cast: if the cast is removed the assignment produces warnings that the 64-bit constant was truncated.

There's nothing wrong with the code (there's nothing wrong with the cast), it's just checkpatch making assumptions that aren't relevant in this special case.

Similarly the test is verifying that `%Ld` is properly handled by the converter: i.e. it is detected and passed through unchanged.  This again is checkpatch making assumptions that any string containing an invalid format specifier in any context must have been meant to be a format specifier:

```
-:4889: WARNING:PRINTF_L: %Ld is non-standard C, use %lld
#4889: FILE: tests/unit/cbprintf/main.c:445:
+	zassert_equal(strncmp("/%Ld/", buf, rc), 0, NULL);
```

Here it's complaining that it's being passed to `strncmp`.  checkpatch is wrong to complain about this.

If you prefer we can eliminate these complaints by (a) not being prepared to support ILP64, and/or (b) not testing handling of undefined format combinations.  But I'd rather just ignore checkpatch's whingeing.
